title: Power from God, not polished words
source_text: Ταῦτα δέ μοι λέλεκται ἀπολογουμένῳ περὶ τῆς κατηγορουμένης ὑπὸ Κέλσου καὶ ἑτέρων ἐν λέξεσιν εὐτελείας τῶν γραφῶν, ἀμαυροῦσθαι δοκούσης ὑπὸ τῆς ἐν συνθέσει λέξεως λαμπρότητος· ἐπεὶ οἱ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς προφῆται Ἰησοῦς τε καὶ οἱ ἀπόστολοι αὐτοῦ ἐνεῖδον τρόπῳ ἀπαγγελίας, οὐ τὰ ἀληθῆ μόνον περιεχούσης ἀλλὰ καὶ δυναμένης ἐπαγαγέσθαι τοὺς πολλοὺς, ἕως προτραπέντες καὶ εἰσαχθέντες ἕκαστος κατὰ δύναμιν ἀναβῶσιν ἐπὶ τὰ ἐν ταῖς δοκούσαις εἶναι εὐτελέσι λέξεσιν ἀποῤῥήτως εἰρημένα. καὶ εἰ χρή γε τολμήσαντα εἰπεῖν, ὀλίγους μὲν ὤνησεν, εἴ γε ὤνησεν, ἡ περικαλλὴς καὶ ἐπιτετηδευμένη Πλάτωνος καὶ τῶν παραπλησίως φρασάντων λέξις· πλείονας δὲ ἡ τῶν εὐτελέστερον ἅμα καὶ πραγματικῶς καὶ ἐστοχασμένως τῶν πολλῶν διδαξάντων καὶ γραψάντων. ἔστι γοῦν ἰδεῖν τὸν μὲν Πλάτωνα ἐν χερσὶ τῶν δοκούντων εἶναι φιλολόγων μόνον, τὸν δὲ Ἐπίκτητον καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν τυχόντων καὶ ῥοπὴν πρὸς τὸ ὠφελεῖσθαι ἐχόντων θαυμαζόμενον, αἰσθομένων τῆς ἀπὸ τῶν λόγων αὐτοῦ βελτιώσεως. καὶ ταῦτά γε οὐκ ἐγκαλοῦντες Πλάτωνί φαμεν (ὁ γὰρ πολὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων κόσμος χρησίμως καὶ τοῦτον ἤνεγκεν) ἀλλὰ καὶ δεικνύντες τὸ βούλημα τῶν εἰπόντων τό· „καὶ ὁ λόγος μου καὶ τὸ κήρυγμά μου οὐκ ἐν πειθοῖς σοφίας λόγοις ἀλλ᾿ ἐν ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως, ἵν᾿ ἡ πίστις ἡμῶν μὴ ᾖ ἐν σοφίᾳ ἀνθρώπων ἀλλ᾿ ἐν δυνάμει θεοῦ.“ φησὶ δ᾿ ὁ θεῖος λόγος οὐκ αὔταρκες εἶναι τὸ λεγόμενον, κἂν καθ᾿ αὐτὸ ἀληθὲς καὶ πιστικώτατον ᾖ, πρὸς τὸ καθικέσθαι ἀνθρωπίνης ψυχῆς, ἐὰν μὴ καὶ δύναμίς τις θεόθεν δοθῇ τῷ λέγοντι καὶ χάρις ἐπανθήσῃ τοῖς λεγομένοις, καὶ αὕτη οὐκ ἀθεεὶ ἐγγινομένη τοῖς ἀνυσίμως λέγουσι. φησὶ γοῦν ὁ προφήτης ἐν ἑξηκοστῷ καὶ ἑβδόμῳ ψαλμῷ ὅτι „κύριος δώσει ῥῆμα τοῖς εὐαγγελιζομένοις δυνάμει πολλῇ.“ ἵν᾿ οὖν ἐπί τινων δοθῇ τὰ αὐτὰ δόγματα εἶναι Ἕλλησι καὶ τοῖς ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἡμῶν, ἀλλ᾿ οὔτι γε καὶ τὰ αὐτὰ δύναται πρὸς τὸ ὑπαγαγέσθαι καὶ διαθεῖναι ψυχὰς κατὰ ταῦτα. διόπερ οἱ ἰδιῶται ὡς πρὸς φιλοσοφίαν Ἑλληνικὴν μαθηταὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐκπεριῆλθον πολλὰ ἔθνη τῆς οἰκουμένης, διατιθέντες, ὡς ὁ λόγος ἐβούλετο, κατ᾿ ἀξίαν ἕκαστον τῶν ἀκουόντων· (οἳ) καὶ ἀνάλογον τῇ ῥοπῇ τοῦ αὐτεξουσίου αὐτῶν πρὸς ἀποδοχὴν τοῦ καλοῦ πολλῷ βελτίους ἐγένοντο.
pass_a_gloss: These things have been said by me in defence (ἀπολογέομαι) of the cheapness/plainness (εὐτέλεια) in diction (λέξις) of the Scriptures (γραφαί), accused (κατηγορέω) by Celsus and others, seeming to be darkened (ἀμαυρόω) by the brilliance (λαμπρότης) of diction in composition (σύνθεσις); since our prophets, both Jesus and his apostles, looked to (ἐνοράω) a manner of report (ἀπαγγελία) not only containing the true things but able to draw (ἐπάγομαι) the many, until, urged on (προτρέπω) and brought in (εἰσάγω), each according to capacity (δύναμις) they ascend (ἀναβαίνω) to the things said ineffably/secretly (ἀπορρήτως) in what seem plain words. And if one must, daring, say it: the very beautiful (περικαλλής) and elaborated (ἐπιτηδεύω) diction of Plato and those phrasing similarly helped (ὀνίνημι) few, if it helped; more, that of those who taught and wrote more plainly and at once practically (πραγματικῶς) and aiming at (στοχάζομαι) the many. One can see Plato in the hands of those seeming to be literary (φιλόλογοι) only, but Epictetus admired even by ordinary people (οἱ τυχόντες) having an inclination (ῥοπή) to being benefited, perceiving the improvement (βελτίωσις) from his words. And we say these things not accusing (ἐγκαλέω) Plato (for the great world (κόσμος) of men usefully bore him too), but showing the intention (βούλημα) of those who said: 'my word and my preaching (κήρυγμα) not in persuasive words of wisdom but in demonstration (ἀπόδειξις) of spirit and power, that our faith be not in wisdom of men but in power of God.' The divine word says the thing spoken, even if in itself true and most persuasive (πιστικώτατος), is not sufficient (αὐτάρκης) to reach (καθικνέομαι) a human soul unless some power from God (θεόθεν) be given to the speaker and grace (χάρις) bloom upon (ἐπανθέω) the things said, and this not without God (ἀθεεί) coming to those speaking effectively (ἀνυσίμως). The prophet says in the sixty-seventh psalm: 'the Lord will give a word (ῥῆμα) to those evangelizing (εὐαγγελίζομαι) with much power.' So granted that in some cases the same doctrines (δόγματα) belong to Greeks and to those from our word, yet they are not able the same to lead (ὑπάγομαι) and dispose (διατίθημι) souls accordingly. Therefore the unlearned, as regards Greek philosophy, disciples of Jesus went round (ἐκπεριέρχομαι) many nations of the inhabited world (οἰκουμένη), disposing, as the word wished, each of the hearers according to worth (ἀξία); who, in proportion (ἀνάλογον) to the inclination of their free will (αὐτεξούσιον) toward acceptance (ἀποδοχή) of the good, became much better.
pass_b_english: I have said this in defence of the plain diction of the Scriptures, for which Celsus and others accuse them, a plainness that seems to be eclipsed by the brilliance of artful composition. For our prophets, and Jesus and his apostles, had in view a way of speaking that not only contains the truth but is also able to draw the many, until, encouraged and led in, each according to his capacity rises to the things spoken in hidden ways in words that seem plain.

And if I must make bold to say it, the very beautiful and studied diction of Plato and of those who wrote in a similar way has benefited few, if it has benefited anyone at all; but the diction of those who taught and wrote more plainly, and at the same time with an eye to the substance and to the many, has benefited more. At any rate, one can see that Plato is in the hands only of those who are thought to be lovers of letters, while Epictetus is admired even by ordinary people who have an inclination toward being helped, since they sense the improvement that comes from his words.

And we say this not to find fault with Plato (for the great world of humankind has usefully produced him too), but also to show the meaning of those who said: “My word and my preaching were not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that our faith might not rest on the wisdom of men but on the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:4–5). The divine word says that what is spoken, even if it is true in itself and most persuasive, is not enough to reach a human soul unless some power is also given from God to the speaker and grace blooms upon what is said; and this grace too does not come without God to those who speak to good effect. So the prophet says in the sixty-seventh Psalm (Psalm 68 in English Bibles): “The Lord will give a word to those who bring good news with great power” (Psalm 68:11).

So, granting that in some cases the same doctrines are held by the Greeks and by those of our teaching, they still do not have the same power to win souls and to shape them according to those doctrines. That is why the disciples of Jesus, unlearned as far as Greek philosophy is concerned, travelled through many nations of the world, shaping each of their hearers according to his worth, as the Word willed; and these hearers, in proportion to the inclination of their free will toward accepting the good, became much better.

choices.choice: 1 Corinthians 2:4–5: Origen’s text reads ἡμῶν (‘our faith’) where the standard New Testament text has ὑμῶν (‘your faith’); translated as Origen quotes it. Origen names the ‘sixty-seventh psalm’ by Septuagint numbering (LXX Psalm 67:12); this is Psalm 68:11 in English Bibles, noted inline. ‘As the Word willed’ renders ὡς ὁ λόγος ἐβούλετο; it could also mean ‘as the teaching (or reason) required’. (οἳ) is Koetschau’s supplement. ‘The prophets, and Jesus and his apostles’ renders οἱ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς προφῆται Ἰησοῦς τε καὶ οἱ ἀπόστολοι αὐτοῦ; the Greek may also be read as ‘our prophets, both Jesus and his apostles’. Possible echo of 1 Corinthians 2:13 in ‘divine word ... power from God’; not cited.
'if one may dare to say it' -> 'if I must make bold to say it' (εἰ χρή γε τολμήσαντα εἰπεῖν)
'but to show' -> 'but also to show' (ἀλλὰ καὶ δεικνύντες)
checked 1 Corinthians 2:4-5 and LXX Psalm 67:12 = Psalm 68:11; both correct
